economy.label: Economy
economy.blurb: Size, growth and stability of what the country produces.

livelihood.label: Livelihoods
livelihood.blurb: What the economy delivers to an ordinary household.

state.label: The state's finances
state.blurb: What the government takes in, spends and owes.

openness.label: Openness
openness.blurb: How connected the economy is to the rest of the world.

human.label: Human development
human.blurb: Health, education and survival - the slowest-moving, hardest-to-fake numbers.

security.label: Conflict & defence
security.blurb: War, armed violence and the means of it. Counted where the fighting happened, which is not the same as who caused it.

politics.label: Politics & rights
politics.blurb: How power is won, constrained and abused. Expert-coded, not government-reported.

indicators.name: GDP per capita
indicators.plain: The country's total output divided by its population, with inflation stripped out so different years compare fairly.
indicators.measures: Market value of goods and services produced per person per year.
indicators.blindspots: An average, so it says nothing about distribution - it rises even if all the gains go to the top 1%. Excludes unpaid work, most of the informal economy, and treats environmental destruction as income.
indicators.gamed: Rebasing the national accounts to a new base year can lift the level overnight without anything real changing. India's 2015 revision and Nigeria's 2014 rebasing are the textbook cases.

indicators.name: GDP growth
indicators.plain: How much bigger the economy got compared with last year.
indicators.measures: Year-on-year percentage change in inflation-adjusted total output.
indicators.blindspots: Very noisy year to year. A high growth rate from a low base is not the same as a high growth rate from a high base - always read it next to the level, not alone.
indicators.gamed: Base-year effects: a terrible year makes the next year's growth look spectacular with no real recovery.

indicators.name: Inflation (consumer prices)
indicators.plain: How much faster prices rose this year than last.
indicators.measures: Annual change in the cost of a fixed basket of consumer goods.
indicators.blindspots: The basket is a national average and rarely matches what a poor household actually buys - food and fuel weigh far more in a poor budget. Mild inflation is normal; the target in most countries is around 2%, not zero.
indicators.gamed: Basket composition and weights are set by the statistical agency. Changing them, or substituting cheaper goods when prices rise, quietly lowers the printed number. Argentina's 2007-2015 statistics are the notorious case.

indicators.name: Unemployment rate
indicators.plain: The share of people who want a job and are actively looking, but do not have one.
indicators.measures: Unemployed as a percentage of the labour force, on ILO-modelled estimates.
indicators.blindspots: Excludes anyone who gave up looking, and counts one hour of paid work a week as employed. In economies with large informal sectors this number is close to meaningless on its own - read it next to labour-force participation.
indicators.gamed: Moving people onto disability or training schemes removes them from the labour force and lowers the rate without creating a single job.

indicators.name: Income inequality (Gini)
indicators.unit: 0 = perfect equality, 100 = one person has everything
indicators.plain: A single number for how unevenly income is shared.
indicators.measures: Statistical dispersion of income across households, from survey data.
indicators.blindspots: Patchy - most countries report it only every few years, so the line will have gaps. Household surveys systematically miss the very rich, so real inequality is almost always worse than the printed figure.

indicators.name: Labour force participation
indicators.plain: The share of working-age people who are either working or looking for work.
indicators.measures: Economically active population as a share of those aged 15 and over.
indicators.blindspots: A fall can mean mass discouragement (bad) or mass enrolment in education (good). It cannot tell you which - check the age breakdown before concluding anything.

indicators.name: Extreme poverty
indicators.plain: The share of people living on less than the international extreme-poverty line.
indicators.measures: Headcount below $2.15 a day, adjusted for what money actually buys locally.
indicators.blindspots: An extremely low bar - someone just above it is still desperately poor. Survey-based and infrequent, so expect gaps and sudden jumps when a new survey lands.

indicators.name: Central government debt
indicators.plain: What the central government owes, measured against the size of the economy.
indicators.measures: Gross central government debt stock as a share of GDP.
indicators.blindspots: Not automatically bad - it depends on the interest rate, the currency it's owed in, and who holds it. Debt in your own currency is a different animal from debt in dollars. Excludes state/provincial debt and public-sector guarantees, which can be enormous.
indicators.gamed: Moving borrowing off-budget into state-owned enterprises keeps it out of this number entirely.

indicators.name: Tax revenue
indicators.plain: How much the government collects in tax, measured against the size of the economy.
indicators.measures: Compulsory transfers to central government, excluding fines and most social security.
indicators.blindspots: Says nothing about who pays. A country can raise this number entirely through sales taxes that fall hardest on the poor. Low figures usually signal a large informal economy rather than generosity.

indicators.name: Health spending (total)
indicators.plain: Everything spent on health care - government and private together - against the size of the economy.
indicators.measures: Current health expenditure as a share of GDP.
indicators.blindspots: Includes out-of-pocket spending, so a high number can mean a failing public system that forces households to pay privately. The US is the extreme example. Always read alongside life expectancy before judging.

indicators.name: Government education spending
indicators.plain: What the government spends on education, against the size of the economy.
indicators.measures: General government expenditure on education, all levels.
indicators.blindspots: Money in, not learning out. Large shares can go to salaries in systems where teacher absenteeism is high. Pair with literacy before drawing conclusions.

indicators.name: Trade openness
indicators.plain: How large the country's trade with the world is, relative to its own economy.
indicators.measures: Exports plus imports of goods and services, divided by GDP.
indicators.blindspots: Small countries score structurally high and big countries structurally low - the US and India will always look closed next to Singapore. Compare a country with its own past, not with a country of a different size.

indicators.name: Foreign direct investment, net inflows
indicators.plain: Money coming in from abroad to buy or build lasting business interests.
indicators.measures: Net inflows of investment acquiring a lasting stake in a foreign enterprise.
indicators.blindspots: Heavily distorted by round-tripping - domestic money routed through a tax haven and back to claim foreign-investor benefits. Mauritius-to-India and Cyprus-to-Russia flows are mostly this.

indicators.name: Life expectancy at birth
indicators.plain: How long a baby born this year would live if today's death rates held for its whole life.
indicators.measures: Period life expectancy at birth, both sexes.
indicators.blindspots: A projection under frozen conditions, not a prediction. Historically dragged down hard by infant deaths, so big early gains often reflect fewer babies dying rather than old people living longer.

indicators.name: Infant mortality
indicators.plain: How many babies out of every thousand die before their first birthday.
indicators.measures: Deaths of infants under one year per 1,000 live births.
indicators.blindspots: One of the hardest numbers to fake and one of the best single summaries of whether a state actually functions. Weak civil registration means poor countries under-count both deaths and births.

indicators.name: Adult literacy
indicators.plain: The share of adults who can read and write a short simple statement.
indicators.measures: Literate population aged 15 and over, as a percentage.
indicators.blindspots: A very low bar that says nothing about comprehension, and often self-reported by the household rather than tested. Reported infrequently, so expect a sparse line.

indicators.name: Urban population
indicators.plain: The share of people living in towns and cities.
indicators.measures: Urban residents as a percentage of total population.
indicators.blindspots: Each country defines 'urban' itself, so cross-country comparison is genuinely unreliable. Reclassifying villages as towns moves this number without anyone relocating.

indicators.name: Population
indicators.plain: How many people live in the country.
indicators.measures: Total resident population, all ages.
indicators.blindspots: Between censuses this is an estimate. Countries that have skipped a census for years are carrying forward assumptions, not counts.

indicators.name: GDP per capita (long run, Maddison)
indicators.plain: The same idea as GDP per capita, but reconstructed by economic historians so it reaches back a century or more.
indicators.measures: Historical real GDP per capita estimates from the Maddison Project Database.
indicators.blindspots: Before roughly 1950 these are scholarly reconstructions, not measurements - the error bars are wide and they get wider the further back you go. Use it for the shape of the trend, never for a precise figure.

indicators.name: Electoral democracy index (V-Dem)
indicators.plain: How free and fair elections actually are, and how much freedom of speech and association surrounds them.
indicators.measures: V-Dem's polyarchy index, aggregated from expert ratings on suffrage, clean elections, elected officials holding real power, and freedom of expression and association.
indicators.blindspots: Built from the judgements of country experts, not from a mechanical count. V-Dem publishes uncertainty intervals for exactly this reason. Small year-to-year wiggles are noise; sustained multi-year moves are the signal.
indicators.gamed: Hard to game directly, which is precisely why it's here - it does not depend on the government reporting on itself.

indicators.name: Liberal democracy index (V-Dem)
indicators.plain: Not just whether elections happen, but whether courts, law and minority rights constrain whoever wins.
indicators.measures: Electoral democracy plus judicial and legislative constraints on the executive and protection of individual liberties.
indicators.blindspots: A country can hold genuinely competitive elections and still score poorly here if the winner faces no real checks. The gap between this and the electoral index is often the most interesting thing on the chart.

indicators.name: Political corruption index (V-Dem)
indicators.plain: How much public officials - in the executive, legislature, courts and bureaucracy - use their position for private gain.
indicators.measures: V-Dem composite across executive, legislative, judicial and public-sector corruption.
indicators.blindspots: Measures perception and expert assessment, not convictions. Convictions measure prosecutorial capacity as much as corruption, which is why this is the more honest of the two.

indicators.name: Political regime type
indicators.unit: 0 closed autocracy, 1 electoral autocracy, 2 electoral democracy, 3 liberal democracy
indicators.plain: A four-way classification of what kind of political system the country had that year.
indicators.measures: Regimes of the World classification, derived from V-Dem indicators.
indicators.blindspots: A step function - it hides gradual erosion until the year a country crosses a threshold. Use the continuous V-Dem indices to see change coming; use this to label it.

indicators.name: GDP, total
indicators.plain: The whole economy's output, inflation stripped out, not divided by population.
indicators.measures: Market value of all goods and services produced in a year.
indicators.blindspots: Size is not prosperity. A large, poor country outranks a small, rich one on this number and always will, which is why it belongs beside GDP per capita rather than instead of it.
indicators.gamed: The same rebasing trick as GDP per capita, with more room to hide: revisions to the deflator move the level without any change in what was produced.

indicators.name: GDP per capita growth
indicators.plain: How much richer the average person got, after accounting for more people.
indicators.measures: Annual change in inflation-adjusted output per person.
indicators.blindspots: An average again. It can be positive while most people get poorer, if the gains are concentrated. Where population is falling it flatters the number for reasons nobody chose.
indicators.gamed: An undercounted population raises output per head arithmetically, so a delayed or disputed census lifts this without anything being produced.

indicators.name: Manufacturing share of output
indicators.plain: How much of the economy is making physical things.
indicators.measures: Value added by manufacturing as a share of total output.
indicators.blindspots: A falling share is not automatically decline - rich countries shift towards services as they get richer. It is bad news only when it falls WITHOUT that shift, which this number alone cannot tell you.
indicators.gamed: Reclassifying assembly or processing work between industry and services moves the share without moving a single factory.

indicators.name: Investment (capital formation)
indicators.plain: How much of what the country earns is put back into building things.
indicators.measures: Gross capital formation - buildings, machinery, infrastructure and inventory changes - as a share of output.
indicators.blindspots: Counts spending, never usefulness. A bridge to nowhere and a needed railway are the same number here, and a construction boom that ends in empty towers looks identical to productive investment while it lasts.
indicators.gamed: Bringing projects forward before an election raises it for a year or two. Unsold inventory also counts as investment.

indicators.name: Youth unemployment
indicators.plain: The share of young people looking for work who cannot find it.
indicators.measures: Modelled ILO estimate of unemployment among 15-24 year olds.
indicators.blindspots: Students sit outside the labour force, so a country that keeps young people in education longer looks better without a single job being created. It also misses underemployment, which is the more common problem in poorer countries.
indicators.gamed: Training schemes and apprenticeships move people out of the count without moving them into work.

indicators.name: Female labour force participation
indicators.plain: The share of adult women in paid work or looking for it.
indicators.measures: Modelled ILO estimate of women aged 15+ who are economically active.
indicators.blindspots: Unpaid household and care work is invisible here, so a fall can mean women being pushed out of paid work, or a household becoming prosperous enough not to need a second income. The number does not distinguish them.
indicators.gamed: Whether subsistence agriculture counts as employment is a definitional choice, and it moves this sharply in largely rural economies.

indicators.name: Income share of the richest 10%
indicators.plain: How much of the country's income goes to the best-off tenth.
indicators.measures: Share of total income or consumption held by the top decile.
indicators.blindspots: The thinnest series in this catalogue - roughly 2,400 observations across 171 countries, so most countries have a scattering of years rather than a line. Household surveys also systematically miss the very richest, so this understates concentration almost everywhere.
indicators.gamed: Survey design decides the answer: what counts as income, whether capital gains are included, and how non-responding rich households are treated.

indicators.name: Military spending
indicators.plain: How much of the economy goes on defence.
indicators.measures: Military expenditure - personnel, operations, procurement, military aid - as a share of output, from SIPRI via the World Bank.
indicators.blindspots: There is no correct level, so up is neither good nor bad. A share of GDP also falls when the economy grows, even if spending rose in cash terms.
indicators.gamed: Paramilitary forces, veterans' benefits and military pensions sit inside or outside the definition depending on the country, and states under pressure move them.

indicators.name: Remittances received
indicators.plain: Money sent home by people working abroad, as a share of the economy.
indicators.measures: Personal transfers and compensation of employees received from abroad.
indicators.blindspots: Counts only money moving through recorded channels, so where informal transfer systems dominate the real figure is far higher. A high number is double-edged: it supports households while saying the work is elsewhere.
indicators.gamed: Not readily gamed by a government, but it jumps when informal flows are formalised - which looks like growth and is a change of plumbing.

indicators.name: Current account balance
indicators.plain: Whether the country earns more from the rest of the world than it spends there. Negative means spending more abroad than it earns.
indicators.measures: Trade, income and transfers with the rest of the world, net, over output.
indicators.blindspots: A deficit is not automatically a problem - it can fund productive investment - and a surplus is not automatically strength, since it can mean weak domestic demand. The direction alone tells you nothing.
indicators.gamed: A large errors-and-omissions line absorbs unrecorded flows, and the balance is revised heavily for years after first publication.

indicators.name: Maternal mortality
indicators.plain: How many women die from causes related to pregnancy and childbirth.
indicators.measures: Modelled estimate of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births.
indicators.blindspots: Modelled, not counted, across most of the world. Where civil registration is weak the figure comes from a statistical model whose uncertainty band is wide enough to swallow small year-to-year changes.
indicators.gamed: Cause-of-death coding decides whether a death is maternal, and deaths outside hospitals are the ones most often missed.

indicators.name: Basic drinking water access
indicators.plain: The share of people with a protected water source within a short walk.
indicators.measures: People using an improved source within a 30-minute round trip, queuing included.
indicators.blindspots: "Basic" is a low bar. It says nothing about whether the water is safe to drink, whether it runs today, or whether a household can afford it - a country can be at 100% here and still have unsafe water.
indicators.gamed: Counting infrastructure built rather than infrastructure working: a standpipe installed and long since broken still counts as a source.

indicators.name: CO2 emissions per person
indicators.plain: How much carbon dioxide the average resident's economy emits in a year.
indicators.measures: Territorial CO2 emissions excluding land use change, per head, on the AR5 accounting basis.
indicators.blindspots: Territorial, so emissions from making goods that are exported count where they are produced, not where they are consumed. Rich countries that import manufactured goods look cleaner than their consumption warrants.
indicators.gamed: Offshoring heavy industry lowers this while global emissions are unchanged - the single largest source of apparent progress in rich countries.

indicators.name: Deaths in armed conflict
indicators.plain: People killed in organised armed conflict on this country's territory.
indicators.measures: UCDP best estimate of deaths from state-based, non-state and one-sided violence, counted where the fighting happened.
indicators.blindspots: Counted where the violence occurred, not who caused it - a country hosting someone else's war carries the number. It also counts deaths from fighting only: famine, displacement and collapsed healthcare kill far more in most wars and appear nowhere here.
indicators.gamed: Not gamed by governments so much as contested by them. UCDP codes from reported incidents, so violence in areas closed to journalists is systematically undercounted, and the low/high estimates can differ severalfold.

indicators.name: Internal armed conflicts
indicators.plain: How many separate internal armed conflicts were active in the country.
indicators.measures: Count of active intrastate conflicts - government against an organised armed group - reaching UCDP's threshold of 25 battle deaths in the year.
indicators.blindspots: A count, so one catastrophic war and one small insurgency both read as "1". The 25-death threshold also means low-level violence disappears entirely, and a conflict that quietens below it looks resolved when it is dormant.
indicators.gamed: Classification is the lever: naming an armed opponent a criminal gang rather than a political organisation keeps a conflict out of this count.

indicators.name: Deaths from terrorism
indicators.plain: People killed in attacks coded as terrorism.
indicators.measures: Fatalities recorded in the Global Terrorism Database, by country and year.
indicators.blindspots: "Terrorism" is a contested label, not a neutral measurement. The same act is coded differently depending on who did it and who is describing it, and state violence is largely outside the definition by construction. Ends 2021.
indicators.gamed: Definitional. Governments have strong reasons to classify political violence as ordinary crime, or ordinary crime as terrorism, and both move this number.

indicators.name: Armed forces personnel
indicators.plain: How many people serve in the armed forces.
indicators.measures: Active duty military personnel, including paramilitaries where they are trained and equipped for military operations.
indicators.blindspots: A headcount says nothing about capability - a large conscript army and a small professional one are not comparable. Read beside military spending, never alone.
indicators.gamed: Where the line falls between police, paramilitary and military is a national choice, and moving a force across it changes the number without changing who is under arms.

indicators.name: Arms imports
indicators.plain: The volume of major weapons brought into the country.
indicators.measures: SIPRI trend-indicator value of major conventional weapons transferred in - a measure of military capability delivered, not of money paid.
indicators.blindspots: TIV is explicitly NOT a price. It cannot be read as spending, compared with a budget, or summed with cash figures. Small arms, ammunition and services are excluded, which is most of what is used in most conflicts.
indicators.gamed: Deliveries are recorded when they arrive, so a single large order lands in one year and makes it a spike that says nothing about a trend.

indicators.name: Arms exports
indicators.plain: The volume of major weapons this country sent to others.
indicators.measures: SIPRI trend-indicator value of major conventional weapons transferred out.
indicators.blindspots: Same unit caveat as arms imports: a capability index, never a sale value. Re-exports and licensed production abroad are attributed in ways that can surprise, and the ultimate end user is often not the recorded recipient.
indicators.gamed: Licensed production overseas moves weapons without moving this number.

indicators.name: Exports
indicators.plain: How much of the economy is sold abroad.
indicators.measures: Exports of goods and services as a share of output.
indicators.blindspots: A share of GDP, so it rises when the domestic economy shrinks. It also says nothing about WHAT is exported - one commodity or a diversified base look identical here, and they are not the same position at all.
indicators.gamed: Re-exports and goods that merely pass through inflate this for entrepot economies, which is why some small states exceed 100%.

indicators.name: Imports
indicators.plain: How much of what the country uses comes from abroad.
indicators.measures: Imports of goods and services as a share of output.
indicators.blindspots: High imports are not weakness and low imports are not strength - both can reflect wealth or crisis. Read against exports, not alone.
indicators.gamed: Under-invoicing to avoid duty, and smuggling, both suppress this in places where enforcement is weak.

indicators.name: High-technology exports
indicators.plain: How much of what the country sells abroad is advanced manufacturing.
indicators.measures: Exports of aerospace, computers, pharmaceuticals, scientific instruments and electrical machinery, as a share of manufactured exports.
indicators.blindspots: Classified by PRODUCT, not by what the country actually did. Assembling imported components counts in full, so a country doing final assembly can outrank one that designed the chip inside.
indicators.gamed: Not usually gamed, but it is routinely quoted as evidence of an innovation economy when it may only show a phone assembly plant.

indicators.name: Government revenue
indicators.plain: Everything the government takes in, except foreign aid.
indicators.measures: Revenue excluding grants - taxes, social contributions, fines, property income.
indicators.blindspots: Central government only in most countries, so states, provinces and municipalities are missing - which understates the true size of the state in federal countries, India and the US among them.
indicators.gamed: One-off asset sales and central bank transfers can be booked as revenue, flattering a single year.

indicators.name: Fiscal balance
indicators.plain: Whether the government took in more than it spent. Negative is a deficit.
indicators.measures: Net lending (+) or net borrowing (-) as a share of output.
indicators.blindspots: A deficit is not automatically mismanagement - borrowing to build something that lasts is different from borrowing to pay salaries, and this number cannot tell them apart. Nor is a surplus automatically good.
indicators.gamed: Off-budget vehicles, state enterprise borrowing and arrears to suppliers all move spending outside the measured balance while the obligation remains.

indicators.name: Public wage bill
indicators.plain: How much of government spending goes on paying its own staff.
indicators.measures: Compensation of employees as a share of total government expense.
indicators.blindspots: High is not automatically waste: teachers and nurses are public employees. A low share can mean an efficient state or a hollowed-out one that has stopped delivering services directly.
indicators.gamed: Outsourcing the same work to contractors moves it out of compensation and into goods and services, with no change in what is done or spent.

indicators.name: Government health spending
indicators.plain: How much the government itself spends on health.
indicators.measures: Domestic general government health expenditure as a share of output - public money only, excluding what households pay themselves.
indicators.blindspots: Spending is not care. It says nothing about whether it reaches patients, and the gap between this and total health spending is what households pay out of pocket - often the more revealing number of the two.
indicators.gamed: Reclassifying water, sanitation or nutrition programmes as health spending raises this without a single extra clinic.

indicators.name: Under-five mortality
indicators.plain: How many children die before their fifth birthday.
indicators.measures: Probability of dying between birth and age five, per 1,000 live births.
indicators.blindspots: Among the hardest numbers to fake and the slowest to move, which is what makes it useful - but it is modelled where registration is weak, and a national figure hides differences between regions and classes that are often larger than differences between countries.
indicators.gamed: Under-registration of births and of infant deaths lowers it, and the two do not cancel out.

indicators.name: Crude death rate
indicators.plain: How many people die each year per thousand of the population.
indicators.measures: Total deaths per 1,000 mid-year population.
indicators.blindspots: CRUDE is the operative word: it is not age-adjusted, so a rich country with many old people has a higher rate than a poor country with a young population. It measures age structure at least as much as health, and comparing two countries on it directly is usually a mistake.
indicators.gamed: Not gamed so much as misused - it is frequently quoted as though it were a health outcome.

indicators.name: Tuberculosis incidence
indicators.plain: How many people newly fall ill with tuberculosis each year.
indicators.measures: Estimated new and relapse TB cases per 100,000 population.
indicators.blindspots: Estimated, not counted. A country that improves its detection can appear to get sicker while actually getting better at finding cases - a rise here may be a working health system rather than a failing one.
indicators.gamed: Reported case notifications depend on how hard a country looks, so reduced screening lowers the notified count while the disease is unchanged.

indicators.name: Suicide rate
indicators.plain: How many people take their own lives each year, per hundred thousand.
indicators.measures: Age-standardised suicide mortality rate.
indicators.blindspots: Systematically undercounted where suicide is criminalised or carries religious stigma, which makes cross-country comparison unreliable in exactly the places the number would matter most. Deaths of undetermined intent are handled differently by different registries.
indicators.gamed: Coroner and certification practice decides the number as much as the underlying rate does.

caveats.note: Automatic political events (leaders, elections, regimes) come from REIGN, whose public release ends in 2021. Curated landmark decisions run to the present but are not exhaustive - absence of a marker is not evidence that nothing happened.
